title: Causes of Migration in an Interconnected World from 1750 to 1900

themes.label: Human-Environment
themes.tooltip: Demographic pressure, famine, and economic displacement pushed people from their home societies; industrial labor demand and available land pulled them to new destinations. Population growth and urbanization reshaped global migration patterns.

themes.label: Economics
themes.tooltip: Industrial capitalism created both free labor migration (workers seeking higher wages) and coerced migration (indentured servitude, convict labor, enslavement) as the global economy required labor in distant production zones.

themes.label: Technology
themes.tooltip: Steam-powered ships dramatically reduced crossing times and costs, making long-distance migration accessible to working-class people for the first time and enabling circular, not just one-way, migration.

tldr: **LO-A: Why people moved: push and pull factors:** Migration in the 19th century was driven by both push factors (famine, poverty, displacement, political persecution) and pull factors (jobs, higher wages, land, opportunity). The Irish Famine (1845–52) killed or displaced 2 million people, a catastrophic push. American economic opportunity, factory wages, prairie farmland, pulled millions across the Atlantic. KC-5.4.I connects migration to demographic changes in both industrialized and non-industrialized societies. **New transportation and urbanization:** Steam-powered ships cut transatlantic crossing times from 6–8 weeks to 10–14 days, dramatically reducing the cost and risk of long-distance migration. KC-5.4.I.B notes that new transportation modes led migrants increasingly to cities, the great urban growth of 19th-century America (New York, Chicago) and Europe (London, Manchester) was partly fueled by migration. Many migrants also returned home periodically, enabled by faster and cheaper transport.

**LO-B: Explain how various economic factors contributed to varied…:** **Free vs. coerced migration, a critical distinction:** KC-5.4.II draws a sharp distinction between voluntary migration (KC-5.4.II.A: many individuals chose freely to relocate in search of work) and coerced migration (KC-5.4.II.B: the global capitalist economy continued to rely on enslaved people, Chinese and Indian indentured servitude, and convict labor). The AP exam tests whether you can identify and distinguish these two patterns. **Indentured servitude and coolie labor, semi-coerced migration:** After the abolition of the Atlantic slave trade and slavery in the British Empire (1833), plantation owners in the Caribbean, South Africa, and Fiji imported workers under indenture contracts: 5–7 years of labor in exchange for passage, wages, and (sometimes) land. Chinese workers (“coolies”) were sent to the Caribbean, South America, and Southeast Asia under often brutal conditions. Indian indentured workers went to Trinidad, Fiji, Natal, and Mauritius. This was legally “voluntary” but often involved deception and coercion in recruitment.
learningObjectives: Explain how various environmental factors contributed to varied patterns of migration from 1750 to 1900
Explain how various economic factors contributed to varied patterns of migration from 1750 to 1900

vocabulary.definition: Push factors drive people away from their home society (famine, war, poverty, political persecution). Pull factors attract migrants to a destination (jobs, land, higher wages, family connections).
vocabulary.importance: The standard framework for analyzing the causes of migration; most 19th-century migrations involved both push and pull factors operating simultaneously.

vocabulary.definition: A pattern in which early migrants from a community establish themselves in a destination and then facilitate the migration of relatives and neighbors, creating a sustained flow between specific origin and destination communities.
vocabulary.importance: Explains why specific immigrant groups clustered in particular cities and neighborhoods; Italian immigrants in Buenos Aires, Irish in Boston, Chinese in San Francisco.

vocabulary.definition: A labor system in which workers signed contracts committing them to 5–7 years of labor for an employer in exchange for passage, food, and wages. Used primarily to replace enslaved labor in British Caribbean, South African, and Pacific colonies after 1833.
vocabulary.importance: Brought Chinese and Indian workers to Trinidad, Fiji, Natal, and Mauritius; classified as “semi-coerced” because contracts were often obtained through deception and working conditions were exploitative.

vocabulary.definition: A catastrophic famine caused by potato blight that killed approximately 1 million Irish people and caused 2 million to emigrate, primarily to the United States, Canada, and Australia. Made worse by British colonial economic policies.
vocabulary.importance: The CED’s primary example of Irish migration; demonstrates how colonial economic relationships could create the push factors driving mass migration.

vocabulary.definition: A term (often derogatory) for Chinese and other Asian indentured or contract workers exported to the Americas, Pacific, and Southeast Asia in the 19th century to work on plantations, railways, and mines.
vocabulary.importance: Represents the semi-coerced migration pattern (KC-5.4.II.B); Chinese workers built the U.S. transcontinental railroad under brutal conditions; others went to Caribbean sugar plantations after British emancipation.

vocabulary.definition: The process by which increasing proportions of a population move to and live in urban areas.
vocabulary.importance: KC-5.4.I.B notes that new modes of transportation led migrants, both internal and international, to relocate increasingly to cities, contributing to the “significant global urbanization of the 19th century.” Industrial cities grew explosively: London grew from 1 million (1800) to 6.7 million (1900).

vocabulary.definition: The pattern of migrants returning, either temporarily or permanently, to their home societies. Enabled by faster and cheaper steam transportation.
vocabulary.importance: KC-5.4.I.B specifically notes that new transportation allowed for “many migrants to return, periodically or permanently, to their home societies”, a significant departure from the essentially one-way migration of earlier periods.

vocabulary.definition: The use of convicted criminals as forced labor, often transported to distant colonies. Britain transported over 160,000 convicts to Australia between 1788 and 1868.
vocabulary.importance: The CED lists convict labor as one form of coerced and semi-coerced labor migration (KC-5.4.II.B); Australia’s early European settlement was substantially built by convict labor.

preTest.question: What is the difference between a “push” factor and a “pull” factor in migration? Give one historical example of each from the period 1750–1900.
preTest.answer: Push factors drive people away from their home society: famine, war, economic collapse, political persecution, natural disaster. The Irish Famine (1845–52), which killed approximately 1 million people and was made worse by British economic policies that continued exporting food from Ireland during the famine, pushed 2 million Irish people to emigrate, primarily to the United States, Canada, and Australia. Pull factors attract migrants to a destination: higher wages, available land, political freedom, family connections (chain migration). The promise of industrial wages in American cities or homestead land on the prairie pulled millions of European migrants to the U.S. throughout the 19th century. Most real migrations involve both: push and pull factors operate simultaneously, and the balance between them determines where people go and how many move.

preTest.question: How did steam-powered transportation change the nature of migration in the 19th century?
preTest.answer: Before steam power, transatlantic crossing took 6–8 weeks by sailing ship, was expensive, physically dangerous, and essentially one-way, few migrants ever returned home. Steam-powered ships cut crossing times to 10–14 days and reduced fares as competition grew. This made migration more accessible to working-class people who couldn’t afford the old fares, dramatically increased migration volumes, and, crucially, made return migration possible. The CED specifically notes (KC-5.4.I.B) that new transportation allowed many migrants to return periodically or permanently to their home societies. Italian workers in Argentina, Japanese agricultural workers in the Pacific, and Lebanese merchants in the Americas could now work abroad for years and then return, a pattern of circular migration that had been impossible or very rare before steam power. This fundamentally changed migration from a one-time life decision to a more fluid economic strategy.

preTest.question: British engineers and geologists went to South Asia and Africa in the 19th century, while Irish peasants went to the United States. Both are classified as “migration”, but what does this comparison reveal about the different character of migration flows in the imperial age?
preTest.answer: The comparison reveals that migration in the imperial age was highly stratified by class and race. British engineers and geologists moved as colonial professionals. They had highly valued skills that the colonial economy needed, they traveled in relative comfort, they enjoyed legal protections as British subjects, and they occupied positions of authority in colonized societies. Irish peasants fled famine and poverty, arrived as unskilled laborers, faced discrimination (the iconic “No Irish Need Apply” signs in American cities), and competed for the lowest-paying industrial jobs. Both groups moved in response to economic opportunities and conditions, but the conditions they fled and the conditions they arrived in were completely different. Imperial-era migration was not a uniform phenomenon. It encompassed privileged colonial professionals, desperate famine refugees, indentured servants, and enslaved people, all under the same analytical label.

preTest.question: Chinese and Indian indentured workers were legally “voluntary” migrants under contract. Why did the CED classify indentured servitude alongside enslavement as “coerced and semi-coerced” migration?
preTest.answer: The legal form (a contract that workers technically signed) did not reflect the reality of recruitment and working conditions. Recruiters in China and India often deceived workers about conditions, wages, and the nature of indenture: many workers did not understand they were committing to 5–7 years of labor in distant tropical colonies. Once indentured, workers were legally bound to their employer and could be imprisoned for leaving or refusing to work. They could not negotiate wages or conditions during the indenture period. Working conditions on Caribbean, Fijian, and Natal plantations were often brutal, with physical punishment and near-slavery conditions. The label “voluntary” applied to a signed contract obtained under deception; the reality was economic coercion and legal bondage for years. This is why historians classify it as “semi-coerced” rather than freely voluntary.

preTest.question: The Irish Famine killed approximately 1 million people in Ireland even as food was being exported from Ireland to Britain. What does this suggest about the relationship between colonialism and migration?
preTest.answer: The Irish Famine was partly a natural disaster (potato blight) but was made catastrophic by colonial economic policy. British landlords continued exporting grain, beef, and other foodstuffs from Ireland to Britain throughout the famine, prioritizing commercial property rights over human survival. The British government’s ideological commitment to free markets prevented effective food relief. The result was that Ireland, a food-producing colony, exported food while its people starved, and then emigrated by the millions. This illustrates a critical connection: colonial economic relationships could generate the very conditions (poverty, food insecurity, land displacement) that created migration push factors. Colonialism didn’t just respond to migration. It often created it.

blocks.text: 🚢 The Scale of 19th-Century Migration: Something New

The 19th century witnessed migration on a scale unprecedented in human history. Between 1820 and 1920, approximately 60 million people left Europe for the Americas, Australia, and South Africa. Millions more moved within Asia, from China and India to Southeast Asia, the Pacific, the Caribbean, and East Africa. Tens of millions moved internally within industrializing nations from rural areas to urban factory centers.

What made this possible? Two revolutions: the **transportation revolution** (steam ships, railways) that dramatically reduced the cost and time of long-distance travel; and the **economic revolution** of industrial capitalism, which created both the demand for labor in industrial and plantation zones and the poverty and displacement that pushed people out of traditional agricultural communities. The CED organizes the causes of this migration into two categories: **environmental/demographic factors** (LO-F, KC-5.4.I) and **economic factors** (LO-G, KC-5.4.II).

Population growth was the fundamental demographic driver. Europe’s population roughly doubled between 1750 and 1850 (from ~140 million to ~270 million), driven by agricultural improvements, the potato (introduced from the Americas), and declining mortality. This population growth exceeded agricultural land availability in many regions, creating a fundamental mismatch: too many people, not enough land and food. KC-5.4.I states directly that migration was influenced by **changes in demographics** in both industrialized and non-industrialized societies that “presented challenges to existing patterns of living.”

The most dramatic push factor was famine. The **Irish Famine** (1845–52) killed approximately 1 million people and caused 2 million to emigrate within a few years, from a population of 8 million. The famine was caused by a potato blight that destroyed the Irish peasantry’s staple food crop. But it was made catastrophic by British colonial economic policy: landlords continued evicting peasants who couldn’t pay rent; the British government adhered to laissez-faire principles and refused to halt food exports from Ireland or provide adequate relief. Irish emigrants flooded into Boston, New York, Philadelphia, and Liverpool, creating the large Irish-American and Irish-British communities that persist today.

Before the Irish Famine, Ireland had a population of about 8 million. By 1900, it had fallen to 4 million, the only European country whose population was smaller at the end of the 19th century than at the beginning. Emigration continued for generations after the famine. Today, more than 30 million Americans identify as having Irish ancestry, about 7 times the current population of Ireland.
🏙️ New Transportation and the City-Bound Migration

Steam-powered ships and railways fundamentally changed migration patterns. A transatlantic crossing that had taken 6–8 weeks by sailing ship now took 10–14 days by steamship, and the cost of passage fell dramatically as competition grew and ships became more fuel-efficient. By 1900, steerage fares from Europe to New York were affordable on a month’s wages.
The CED highlights two specific effects of new transportation on migration (KC-5.4.I.B):

items: **Urban migration:** Both internal and international migrants increasingly relocated to cities, because cities were where the industrial jobs were and where transportation connected them to the outside world. London grew from 1 million people in 1800 to 6.7 million in 1900. New York grew from 60,000 in 1800 to 3.4 million in 1900. This pattern contributed to what the CED calls “significant global urbanization of the 19th century.”

**Return migration:** Faster and cheaper transportation made it possible for migrants to return to their home societies, periodically or permanently. The CED specifically lists **Japanese agricultural workers in the Pacific**, **Lebanese merchants in the Americas**, and **Italian industrial workers in Argentina** as examples of return migrants. Italian men often worked in Argentine factories or Uruguayan construction during the Southern Hemisphere summer and returned to Italy in the European summer. They were called “swallows” (*golondrinas*).

blocks.text: 💸 Economic Causes: Free and Coerced Migration

The CED draws a critical distinction between two types of economic migration (KC-5.4.II): **freely chosen migration** and **coerced or semi-coerced migration**. Both were driven by the global capitalist economy’s demand for labor, but the conditions under which people moved were profoundly different.

**Freely chosen migration** (KC-5.4.II.A): Many individuals chose voluntarily to relocate, often in search of work. The CED’s examples include **British engineers and geologists** going to South Asia and Africa (skilled professionals following colonial opportunities) and **Irish migrants to the United States** (though the Irish case blurs the line between “free” and “coerced”, famine refugees had little real choice). Italian workers in Argentina, Chinese merchants in Southeast Asia, and Lebanese traders in the Americas all represent broadly voluntary economic migration.
**Coerced and semi-coerced migration** (KC-5.4.II.B): The global capitalist economy continued to rely on forced and semi-forced labor migration. The CED identifies three main forms:

items: **Enslavement:** The Atlantic slave trade was officially banned by Britain in 1807 and the U.S. in 1808, but illegal slave trading continued. Within Africa, enslavement and the Indian Ocean slave trade persisted throughout the 19th century. Even after emancipation in the British Empire (1833) and the Americas (U.S. 1865, Brazil 1888, Cuba 1886), formerly enslaved people faced economic coercion through sharecropping and debt systems that limited their freedom.

**Chinese and Indian indentured servitude:** After British emancipation (1833), Caribbean and other plantation owners needed replacement labor. They turned to **indentured workers** from China and India, who signed 5–7 year contracts for passage and wages. Hundreds of thousands of Indian workers went to Trinidad, Guyana, Fiji, Mauritius, and Natal. Chinese workers went to Peru (guano islands), Cuba, the United States (transcontinental railroad), and Southeast Asia. Recruitment was often deceptive and working conditions were brutal.

**Convict labor:** Britain transported over 160,000 convicted criminals to Australia between 1788 and 1868. This convict transportation served both as punishment and as a labor supply for colonial development, forced migration in service of imperial economic needs.

blocks.text: Topic 6.6 covers TWO learning objectives (LO-F and LO-G) and two sets of KCs (KC-5.4.I and KC-5.4.II). LO-F focuses on environmental and demographic factors (population growth, famine, urbanization, transportation). LO-G focuses on economic factors (free labor migration vs. coerced migration including enslavement, indentured servitude, convict labor). Know the CED’s illustrative examples: return migrants (Japanese agricultural workers, Lebanese merchants, Italian workers in Argentina); free migrants (Irish to U.S., British engineers to South Asia/Africa); coerced migrants (enslaved peoples, Chinese and Indian indentured workers, convict labor).

About 140,000 Chinese workers were brought to Peru’s guano islands (the Chincha Islands) under indenture contracts in the 1850s–70s. Working conditions were among the worst of any labor system in the world: workers shoveled guano in suffocating ammonia fumes, were subject to physical punishment, and had a death rate approaching 50%. The guano trade made Peru wealthy; the workers who made it possible were worked nearly to death. This is one reason historians classify indentured servitude as “semi-coerced” rather than freely voluntary.

multipleChoice.stimulus: "Between 1845 and 1852, a potato blight destroyed the staple food crop of Ireland’s largely Catholic peasant population. Approximately 1 million people died of starvation and disease. During the same period, food exports from Ireland, primarily grain and cattle for English markets, continued, as landlords enforced rent payments and evictions. An estimated 2 million Irish people emigrated, primarily to the United States."
multipleChoice.question: The Irish emigration described in the passage is BEST categorized as which type of migration?
options: Migration driven by demographic crisis partly created and worsened by colonial economic policies
Coerced migration organized by the British government to relieve population pressure in Ireland
Purely voluntary migration driven by economic opportunity in the United States
Chain migration in which early Irish migrants attracted relatives by sending positive reports from America
multipleChoice.explanation: The passage shows the interaction of natural disaster (blight) with colonial economic conditions (continued food exports, landlord evictions, inadequate relief) that made the famine catastrophic and created overwhelming push factors for emigration. The Irish famine illustrates KC-5.4.I: migration was “influenced by changes in demographics that presented challenges to existing patterns of living.” (C) is wrong, the primary cause was famine push, not American opportunity pull. (B) is wrong, the British government did not organize the emigration. (D) is partially true about later migration patterns but not the primary cause described in the passage.

multipleChoice.stimulus: "The new steam-powered ships and railway networks of the 19th century not only moved goods but transformed the scale and character of human migration. A crossing that had taken 6–8 weeks by sailing ship now took 10–14 days, and ticket prices fell dramatically. Migrants who once left their home communities permanently could now contemplate working abroad temporarily and returning home seasonally or after saving enough money."
multipleChoice.question: The development described in the passage most directly illustrates which historical pattern?
options: The Industrial Revolution reduced demand for migrant labor by automating most industrial jobs
European governments used faster ships to enforce stricter controls on emigration
New transportation modes enabled circular and return migration patterns in addition to permanent emigration
Improved transportation primarily benefited skilled professional migrants rather than working-class laborers
multipleChoice.explanation: The passage describes exactly what KC-5.4.I.B identifies: new transportation modes made it possible for migrants to return periodically or permanently to their home societies, enabling the “swallow” pattern (Italian workers in Argentina who returned seasonally), Lebanese merchants in the Americas, and Japanese agricultural workers in the Pacific. (A) is the opposite of what happened, industrialization increased labor demand. (B) is not what the passage describes. (D) is wrong, lower prices specifically made migration accessible to working-class people.

multipleChoice.stimulus: "After the British Emancipation Act of 1833 freed enslaved people in British colonies, Caribbean plantation owners faced a labor shortage as formerly enslaved people refused to work on the same plantations that had held them. To replace this labor supply, British colonial authorities arranged for Indian workers to sign 5-year indenture contracts, receiving passage and minimal wages in exchange for labor on Caribbean sugar plantations."
multipleChoice.question: The labor system described in the passage is best characterized as which of the following?
options: Freely voluntary migration, as workers signed legal contracts of their own accord
A form of semi-coerced migration that replaced enslaved labor while preserving the plantation system’s need for controlled, bound labor
Chain migration, as established Indian communities in the Caribbean attracted relatives from India
An example of the British government’s commitment to improving labor standards in its colonies after emancipation
multipleChoice.explanation: Indentured servitude was legally “voluntary” (workers signed contracts) but was semi-coerced because recruitment often involved deception, workers had no ability to leave during indenture, and working conditions resembled enslavement. KC-5.4.II.B classifies it as “semi-coerced” labor migration alongside enslavement and convict labor. The passage also explicitly notes that it was used to replace enslaved labor, preserving the plantation system’s economic structure after emancipation. (A) overstates the freedom of choice. (C) is about a different type of migration not described. (D) misrepresents intent, the system was about labor supply, not worker welfare.

multipleChoice.stimulus: "In the second half of the 19th century, London’s population grew from 2.3 million (1850) to 6.7 million (1900). Chicago’s population grew from 30,000 (1850) to 1.7 million (1900). Both cities drew internal migrants from rural areas and international migrants from Europe and elsewhere."
multipleChoice.question: The demographic pattern shown in the data BEST illustrates which aspect of 19th-century migration?
options: New transportation technology enabled mass migration from cities to rural areas in search of land
International migration was primarily circular, with most migrants eventually returning to their countries of origin
Population growth in industrial cities was primarily the result of declining death rates rather than migration
Both internal and international migrants increasingly relocated to cities, contributing to significant global urbanization (KC-5.4.I.B)
multipleChoice.explanation: The data shows the explosive urban growth that KC-5.4.I.B identifies: migrants, both internal and international, relocated to cities, creating the “significant global urbanization of the 19th century.” London and Chicago are examples of industrial cities that drew migrants from wide geographic areas. (A) is the reverse of what happened. (B) is not what the data shows. (C) may be partly true but is not what the CED identifies as the key pattern, the passage specifically mentions that “both cities drew internal migrants from rural areas and international migrants.”

multipleChoice.stimulus: "Chinese laborers on the U.S. transcontinental railroad (completed 1869) were paid approximately two-thirds the wages of comparable white workers, were assigned the most dangerous tasks (including drilling through granite and handling nitroglycerin in the Sierra Nevada), and lived in segregated camps without the benefits and land grants offered to white workers."
multipleChoice.question: The conditions described for Chinese railroad workers BEST illustrate which combination of migration characteristics from KC-5.4?
options: Freely voluntary migration and equal treatment in a labor market that rewarded skill
Semi-coerced migration under racially discriminatory conditions, consistent with the CED’s classification of Chinese labor migration as coerced or semi-coerced
Return migration, as Chinese workers were temporarily employed before returning to China after railroad completion
Chain migration organized through established Chinese communities in California who recruited workers from China
multipleChoice.explanation: The passage shows structural discrimination, lower wages for equivalent or harder work, dangerous assignments, exclusion from benefits, that reflects the semi-coerced character of Chinese labor migration in the 19th century. KC-5.4.II.B classifies Chinese labor migration as coerced/semi-coerced because workers operated under conditions of legal and racial discrimination that severely limited their economic freedom. (A) is directly contradicted by the wage and treatment disparities described. (C) is partially accurate but not the pattern the passage primarily illustrates. (D) describes a recruitment mechanism but not the conditions of the work.

saq.context: “Migration in many cases was influenced by changes in demographics in both industrialized and unindustrialized societies that presented challenges to existing patterns of living. Because of the nature of new modes of transportation, both internal and external migrants increasingly relocated to cities.”, KC-5.4.I
saq.directions: Answer parts A, B, and C. Each requires a separate short response. Do not write a full essay.

parts.label: Part A
parts.task: Briefly describe ONE specific way demographic or environmental changes contributed to migration patterns in the period 1750–1900.
parts.sampleAnswer: Population growth in Europe, driven by improved agricultural productivity and declining mortality, created pressure on available agricultural land by the mid-19th century. In Ireland, a population of 8 million depended heavily on the potato as a staple crop, when blight destroyed the potato harvest between 1845 and 1852, approximately 1 million people died and 2 million emigrated within a decade. This demographic crisis was amplified by British colonial economic policies that allowed food exports to continue during the famine and prioritized landlord property rights over peasant survival. The Irish Famine exemplifies KC-5.4.I: demographic changes (population growth, food insecurity) combined with colonial conditions to create overwhelming push factors that drove mass emigration.

parts.label: Part B
parts.task: Briefly explain the difference between freely chosen migration and coerced migration in the period 1750–1900, using ONE specific example of each type.
parts.sampleAnswer: Freely chosen migration (KC-5.4.II.A) describes movement where individuals had genuine choice: British engineers going to South Asia and Africa for career advancement in colonial industries, or Italian workers going to Argentina in search of higher wages with the expectation of returning home. These migrants had agency, legal rights, and some ability to choose their conditions. Coerced and semi-coerced migration (KC-5.4.II.B) describes movement under compulsion or deception: Indian indentured workers who signed 5–7 year contracts often obtained through deceptive recruitment, committing themselves to years of bound labor on Caribbean plantations under conditions resembling enslavement. The key distinction is not just legal form (both signed something resembling a contract) but whether workers could realistically refuse, leave, or negotiate conditions during the labor commitment.

parts.label: Part C
parts.task: Briefly explain ONE way new transportation technology changed migration patterns in the period 1750–1900.
parts.sampleAnswer: Steam-powered ships dramatically reduced transatlantic crossing times from 6–8 weeks to 10–14 days and lowered ticket prices to levels accessible to working-class migrants. This made return migration possible for the first time: Italian agricultural workers could travel to Argentina for the Southern Hemisphere harvest season and return to Italy for the European summer, a seasonal circular migration pattern the CED calls “swallows” (*golondrinas*). KC-5.4.I.B specifically notes that new transportation “allowed for many migrants to return, periodically or permanently, to their home societies.” This transformed migration from a permanent, irreversible decision into a more flexible economic strategy that sustained ongoing cultural and economic connections between sending and receiving communities.

outline.label: Evidence for environmental/demographic causes
outline.text: Irish Famine: potato blight + colonial policy = 2 million emigrants; European population growth exceeded agricultural land in many regions; New transportation connected rural migrants to cities globally; Urbanization driven partly by rural push from agricultural displacement

outline.label: Evidence for economic causes
outline.text: Industrial labor demand pulled migrants to specific factory cities; Plantation labor needs drove indentured servitude systems (Chinese/Indian workers); Capital investment in railways and infrastructure in specific regions pulled migrants there; British engineers went to colonies because colonial economies needed skilled labor at premium wages; Coerced labor migration (enslavement, indenture, convict labor) entirely economically driven

leq.prompt: Evaluate the extent to which economic factors, rather than environmental and demographic factors, drove migration patterns from 1750 to 1900.
leq.note: Write a full essay with a thesis, contextualization, evidence, and historical reasoning. Use causation as your primary skill. A strong response will engage with both categories of causes and argue a qualified claim about their relative importance.
leq.thesisExample: Strong thesis: “Although environmental and demographic factors, famine, population growth, displacement, created the initial push conditions that made migration necessary for millions of people, economic factors were ultimately more significant as migration causes because they determined where people could go, how they traveled, and whether they moved as free workers or bound laborers, shaping the structural character of migration flows in ways that demographic pressure alone could not.”

discussionQuestions.question: 1. The CED distinguishes between “freely” chosen and “coerced” migration, but many historians argue this distinction oversimplifies reality. Using the Irish Famine as an example, is migration “free” if the alternative is starvation?
discussionQuestions.modelAnswer: The question of what makes migration “free” is genuinely difficult. The Irish who emigrated during the famine technically chose to leave rather than stay. They weren’t physically forced onto ships. But they were fleeing famine partly created and worsened by colonial economic policy. When the alternative to emigration is starvation, the “choice” to leave is made under extreme duress that constrains meaningful freedom. This suggests that the free-vs-coerced distinction is a spectrum rather than a binary. The Irish case sits uncomfortably in the middle: legally voluntary, but structurally coerced by colonial conditions. The CED’s distinction is useful for analytical purposes, distinguishing between a British engineer going to India for career advancement and an Indian indentured worker going to Trinidad under a contract obtained through deception, but it should not obscure the many cases where “voluntary” migration was made under conditions of extreme economic and political pressure.

discussionQuestions.question: 2. Steam transportation made return migration possible for the first time. Why does this matter for understanding how migration affected both sending and receiving societies?
discussionQuestions.modelAnswer: Return migration changed migration from a permanent rupture to a sustained relationship between communities. When migrants could return, they brought back money (remittances could fund family businesses, pay for siblings’ education, or buy land in the home community), new ideas (exposure to different political systems, new technologies, different social norms), and maintained cultural connections (language, food, religion). This two-way flow meant sending societies were permanently transformed by the experience of migration even for families whose members returned. For receiving societies, temporary migrants who returned home created different demographic patterns than permanent settlers: they contributed economically without fully integrating culturally. The Italian “swallows” in Argentina who returned home each season left less permanent cultural marks on Argentine society than the Italian immigrants who stayed permanently and whose descendants became Argentine.

discussionQuestions.question: 3. Why did the British Empire replace enslaved labor with indentured servitude after emancipation (1833) rather than paying free wages competitive enough to attract voluntary workers? What does this tell us about the economic logic of the plantation system?
discussionQuestions.modelAnswer: The plantation system’s profitability depended on extremely cheap, controlled labor that could not leave and could not bargain collectively. After emancipation, formerly enslaved people in the Caribbean exercised their new freedom by refusing to work on plantations that had imprisoned and brutalized them for generations, understandably. Free wage labor, if market rates were paid, would have dramatically increased labor costs and reduced plantation profits. Indentured servitude preserved the economic logic of the plantation system at lower cost than free wages: workers were legally bound for years, could not leave, had limited ability to bargain, and could be punished for contract violations. The “choice” between full free-market wages and indentured servitude was never seriously considered by plantation owners. The system reveals that the plantation economy was built on the ability to pay below-market wages to coerced labor, and that the shift from slavery to indenture was about preserving this structure, not about improving workers’ conditions.
